record.original_question: Which finite graphs can be represented as tangency graphs of spheres in three-dimensional space?

evidence.quote: Question 8.7 Which graphs can be represented by spheres in 3-space?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Call a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$ a *sphere tangency graph in $\mathbb{R}^3$* if there exists a family $\{B_v : v\in V\}$ of round balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with pairwise disjoint interiors, indexed by the vertices of $G$, such that for every pair of distinct vertices $u,v\in V$, the boundary spheres $\partial B_u$ and $\partial B_v$ are tangent (i.e. meet in exactly one point) if and only if $\{u,v\}\in E$.

Give a characterization of the class of finite simple graphs that arise as sphere tangency graphs in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
artifact.status_search_result: While the analogous 2-dimensional problem is settled by the Koebe–Andreev–Thurston circle packing theorem (planar graphs), the characterization of graphs representable as tangency graphs of interior-disjoint balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is widely regarded as an open problem. Sphere contact/tangency configurations in 3-space remain an active area of investigation, with partial results on edge counts and special families but no known full combinatorial characterization.

status_evidence.title: Sphere packings in 3-space
status_evidence.snippet: One of the most basic questions on contact graphs is to find the maximum number of edges that a contact graph of a packing of n unit balls can have in Euclidean 3-space.
status_evidence.claim: Even basic extremal questions on sphere contact graphs in 3-space are still under investigation, indicating that a full characterization is not known.
